children: Indonesia's central bank kept interest rates unchanged Wednesday, assessing the impact of rupiah-support measures as currency risks flared again.

Bank Indonesia held its benchmark seven-day reverse repo rate at 5.75%, in line with expectations, following consecutive rate increases in May and June. Nine of 10 economists polled by The Wall Street Journal expected no change, while one expected a 25-basis-point increase.
The central bank also kept its overnight deposit facility rate at 4.75% and its lending facility rate at 6.50%.

The move is consistent with BI's strategy to "stabilize the rupiah amid still-high external pressures, keep inflation within its target range and support continued economic growth," Gov. Destry Damayanti said in a press conference.

The decision comes as renewed escalation in the Middle East pushed up energy prices, raising expectations that central banks will need to tighten further to keep price growth in check and currencies steady.
Last week, both the Federal Reserve and the Bank of Japan raised rates.

Bank Indonesia has already delivered 100 basis points of rate hikes this year, and inflation remains on target. It has also intervened repeatedly to support the rupiah--its traditional core objective--with some degree of success.
But analysts still see scope for more tightening ahead.

Goldman Sachs economists noted that though the rupiah appreciated against the dollar since early August, it has given back some gains in recent weeks as oil prices climbed and the Fed outlook turned more hawkish.

"With FX conditions nonetheless more stable, we think policymakers will prefer to preserve optionality for now and hope for the best," GS said, pushing back its rate-hike forecasts to one move in the fourth quarter, followed by another in the first quarter of next year.
Analysts at BMI, a unit of Fitch Solutions, pointed out that the rupiah is still about 6% weaker against the greenback year-to-date, despite BI's expanded foreign-exchange support measures.

Domestic policy concerns, a prolonged U.S.-Iran conflict and El Nino-related weather disruptions all pose threats to the rupiah, increasing the likelihood of further rate increases this year, BMI said.
